status_summary: No separation of U.S. Cyber Command from the National Security Agency has occurred, and the administration has kept one officer in both roles. After Gen. Timothy Haugh, who led both organizations, was fired in April 2025, The Record reported on 2025-05-14 that no decision on a split had been made and on 2025-09-09, citing unnamed sources, that senior officials had dropped a possible split without a formal presidential document. On 2026-03-10 the Senate confirmed Gen. Joshua Rudd, 71 to 29 (roll call vote 49 on PN711), to lead NSA and also serve as dual-hat leader of Cyber Command, after he told his 2026-01-15 confirmation hearing that he would keep assessing the arrangement. Under an earlier defense policy law, as described by The Record, a split requires a joint certification by the Defense Secretary and the Joint Chiefs Chairman, and no certification, decision to split or separation plan was found through 2026-10-18.

timeline.event: The Record reports that weeks after Gen. Haugh's firing the administration had not decided whether to split the roles; acting leader Lt. Gen. Hartman and Chairman Gen. Caine favored keeping the dual-hat, and a split would require a joint certification under an earlier defense policy law.

The Record reports, citing unnamed sources, that senior officials dropped a possible split of the roles without a presidential memo, judging that ending the dual-hat could take up to three years; a White House official said no long-term decisions had been made. It adds that the Defense Secretary told senators in June 2025 that the status quo held while reserving the right to review it, and that the Joint Chiefs Chairman wrote that the arrangement should remain.

At his Senate Armed Services confirmation hearing, Lt. Gen. Joshua Rudd, nominated to lead both NSA and Cyber Command, cites the arrangement's effectiveness and says he would keep assessing whether the dual-hat is the most effective structure; no decision or timeline is reported.

The Senate confirms Lt. Gen. Joshua M. Rudd (PN711) to be a general in the Army, 71 to 29, on roll call vote 49 (cloture had been invoked 68 to 28 on 2026-03-09). The Washington Examiner reports he will lead both the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command in a dual-hat arrangement after about a year without Senate-confirmed leaders at both agencies. SecurityWeek (2026-03-11) also reports the confirmation covers leading both organizations.
